To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified four vibrational progress ions of the N2, N4, and N3 centers in diamond by photoluminescence ( PL) spectra excited in the range of 150–260 nm.
the photoluminescent properties of nitrogen defects in type IaAB natural diamond are identified with photoluminescent spectra excited in the 150-260nm region.
the photoluminescent properties of diamond are strongly dependent on excitation wavelength.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to diamond characterization using the photoluminescent excitation spectra of nitrogen-related defects in diamond.
the development of novel methods of diamond characterization and identification of the type of diamond.
the identification of nitrogen defects in type IaAB natural diamond with PL excited in the 150-260-nm region and with the analysis of the PLE spectra at a temperature of ∼13 K.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PLE spectra of the N2 and N3 defects are the best indicators for identifying type IaAB diamond, and the PLE spectra for the N3 defect are the best indicators of type Ib diamond.
the PLE spectra excited in the range of 160-260 nm are a powerful tool for the identification of nitrogen defects in type IaAB diamond.
the PL of diamond can be used to identify and characterize diamond samples, and the PL of diamond excited in the 150-260-nm region provides a new method to characterize diamond samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the N2, N4, and N3 centers are identified in diamond of type Ib, and N3, N2, and N4 defects in diamond of type IIa, IaAB, and IaB, respectively.
we have identified four nitrogen defects in diamond, N2, N4, N3, B', and their vibrational progressions, and have determined the energy levels of these defects.
the PL spectra of natural diamond at 13 and 300 K excited in the 150-260-nm region are a powerful technique for the analysis and identification of nitrogen defects in type-IaAB diamonds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PL spectra of diamond excited at 160-240 can be used to identify the type of nitrogen defect in diamond.
the N2 and N4 centers can be identified in diamond by the use of PL excited in the region from 160 to 240 nm.
we have been able to identify the N3 center for the first time in natural diamond.
